'''''Plantago major''''', the '''greater plantain''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the plantain family [[Plantaginaceae]]. It is native to Eurasia and temperate Africa, and widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] elsewhere.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=Plants of the World Online |website=Plants of the World Online |date=2007-08-18 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:321286-2 |access-date=2026-07-06}}</ref><ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web |title=Greater Plantain ''Plantago major'' L. |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.p08 |access-date=2026-07-06}}</ref>

Greater plantain is not closely related to the fruit also known as [[Cooking banana|plantain]], which is a type of [[banana]].

==Description==
''Plantago major'' is a [[herbaceous]], [[perennial plant]] with a [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] of [[leaves]] {{convert|15–30|cm|in|0|abbr=off}}, exceptionally {{convert|70|cm|in|0|abbr=off}},<ref>Schmelzer, G.H. & Gurib-Fakim, A. (Editors), 2008. [https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Randolph-Arroo/publication/317510018_Plant_Resources_of_Tropical_Africa_111_Medicinal_plants_1/ Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 11(1)- Medicinal plants 1.] PROTA Foundation, Wageningen, Netherlands / Backhuys Publishers, Leiden, Netherlands / CTA, Wageningen, Netherlands. 791 pp.</ref> in diameter.<ref name="pakistan" /><ref name="blamey">{{cite book |last1=Blamey |first1=Marjorie |last2=Grey-Wilson |first2=C. |title=The illustrated flora of Britain and northern Europe |publisher=Hodder & Stoughton |publication-place=London |date=1989 |isbn=0-340-40170-2 |pages=380–381}}</ref> Each leaf is oval-shaped, {{convert|3–18|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2–11|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad, rarely up to {{convert|30|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|21|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} broad, with an acute apex, a smooth margin, and a distinct [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] almost as long as the leaf itself.<ref name="FoC">{{cite web |title=''Plantago major'' in Flora of China @ efloras.org |website=eFloras.org Home |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200022050 |access-date=2026-07-06}}</ref> There are three to seven (rarely nine) conspicuous veins over the length of the leaf.<ref name="FoC"/><ref>Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref> The [[flower]]s are small, greenish-brown with purple [[stamen]]s, produced in a dense spike {{convert|1–20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} (rarely to {{convert|40|cm|in|abbr=on}}) long on top of a stem {{convert|2–18|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} (rarely to {{convert|70|cm|in|abbr=on}}) tall; flowering is from May to October in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="FoC"/><ref name="pakistan" /><ref name="blamey" />

Greater plantain is [[wind-pollinated]] and propagates primarily by seeds, which are held on the long, narrow spikes which rise well above the foliage.<ref name=blamey/><ref>{{cite book|author=Sauer, Leslie Jones|title=The Once and Future Forest|year=1998|publisher=Island Press|isbn=978-1-55963-553-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bC76cUM721sC|page=49}}{{verify source|date=July 2012}}</ref> Each plant can produce up to 20,000 seeds, which are very small and oval-shaped, with a bitter taste.<ref name="Samuelsen-2000-p1">{{cite journal|author=Samuelsen, Anne Berit|title=The traditional uses, chemical constituents and biological activities of ''Plantago major'' L. A review|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|volume=77|issue=1–2|pages=1–21|date=July 2000|doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(00)00212-9|pmid=10904143|issn=0378-8741|pmc=7142308}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
There are three [[subspecies]]:<ref name="POWO"/><ref name="flora" />
*''Plantago major'' subsp. ''major''. Occurs throughout the range of the species.<ref name="POWO-major">{{cite web |title=''Plantago major'' subsp. ''major'' |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77227281-1 |access-date=2026-07-06}}</ref>
*''Plantago major'' subsp. ''intermedia'' (Gilib.) Lange. Occurs in Europe, northwest Africa, and northern Asia, but its distribution is not well studied; it grows in wetter habitats, including saline locations such as saltmarshes and beside [[road salt|salted roads]].<ref name="POWO-intermedia">{{cite web |title=''Plantago major'' subsp. ''intermedia'' (Gilib.) Lange |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:60471524-2 |access-date=2026-07-06}}</ref><ref name="PlantAtlas-intermedia">{{cite web |title=''Plantago major'' subsp. ''intermedia'' (Gilib.) Lange |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.fwq |access-date=2026-07-06}}</ref> It differs in having finely hairy, narrower, 3–5-veined leaves.<ref name="blamey" />
*''Plantago major'' subsp. ''winteri'' (Wirtg.) W.Ludw. Occurs in central and northeastern Europe.<ref name="POWO-winteri">{{cite web |title=''Plantago major'' subsp. ''winteri'' (Wirtg.) W.Ludw. |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77251828-1 |access-date=2026-07-06}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Greater plantain is native to almost all of Europe (Iceland excepted), northern and central Asia, and northern and southern Africa.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=flora>''Flora Europaea'': [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Plantago&SPECIES_XREF=major&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Plantago major'']</ref><ref name=pakistan>''Flora of Pakistan'': [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=200022050 ''Plantago major'']</ref> and has become widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] elsewhere in the world.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 16 December 2017}}</ref>

The ability of greater plantain to survive frequent trampling and colonise compacted soils makes it important for [[soil rehabilitation]]. Its roots break up [[hardpan]] surfaces, while simultaneously holding together the soil to prevent [[erosion]].<ref name="Tilford-1998-p163">{{cite book|author1=Tilford, Gregory L. |author2=Gladstar, Rosemary |title=From Earth to Herbalist: An Earth-Conscious Guide to Medicinal Plants|publisher=Mountain Press|year=1998|isbn=978-0-87842-372-9|page=163|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z9VXQ1O1nYEC&pg=PA163}}</ref> The seeds are a common contaminant in [[cereal]] grain and other crop seeds. As a result, it now has a nearly worldwide distribution.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=grin/> ''Plantago major'' grows in lawns and fields, along roadsides, and in other areas that have been disturbed by humans. It does particularly well in [[soil compaction|compacted]] or disturbed soils, but can also occur in undisturbed grassland.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/>

===Other names===
As a result of its wide occurrence, ''Plantago major'' has many vernacular names. In addition to greater plantain, other recorded vernacular names include broadleaf plantain, common plantain, broad-leaved plantain, cart track plant, dooryard plantain, greater plantago, healing blade, hen plant, lambs foot, roadweed, roundleaf plantain, snakeroot, waybread, wayside plantain, and white man's footprint.<ref>{{cite book |last= Britton|first= Nathaniel Lord| author-link= Nathaniel Lord Britton|author2=Addison Brown |title=An Illustrated Flora of the Northern United States and Canada, Volume 3|edition= second|year= 1913|publisher= Dover Publications, inc.|page=245}}</ref> ''Plantago major'' is believed to be one of the first plants to reach North America after European colonisation. Reportedly brought to the Americas by Puritan colonists, greater plantain was known among some Native American peoples by the name "white man's footprint", because it thrived in the disturbed and damaged ecosystems surrounding European settlements.<ref>{{cite book|author=Duke, James|title=Handbook of Edible Weeds|publisher=CRC Press|year=2001|isbn=978-0-8493-2946-3|page=150|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rVrteo-8cI0C&pg=PA150}}</ref> 

==Uses==
The leaves are edible and can be used to stop bleeding, soothe burns and insect bites.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Braiding Sweetgrass |publisher=Milkweed Editions |year=2013 |isbn=9781571313560 |location=Minneapolis, MN |pages=213-214}}</ref> The mature plant contains pliable and tough [[Fiber crop|fibres]] that can be used in survival situations to make small cords, [[fishing line]], [[Surgical suture|sutures]], or [[Braid#Industrial history and use|braiding]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Tilford, Gregory L.|title=Edible and Medicinal Plants of the West|publisher=Mountain Press|year=1997|isbn=978-0-87842-359-0|page=112|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P_s7sD11RM8C&pg=PA112}}</ref> Some [[cultivar]]s are planted as [[Ornamental plant|ornamentals]] in [[garden]]s, including 'Rubrifolia' with purple leaves, and 'Variegata' with [[variegation|variegated]] leaves.<ref name="rhs">Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}</ref> The leaves are edible as a [[Leaf vegetable|salad green]] when young and tender, but they quickly become tough and fibrous as they get older. The older leaves can be cooked in stews.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Scott, Timothy Lee |author2=Buhner, Steven Harrod |title=Invasive Plant Medicine: The Ecological Benefits and Healing Abilities of Invasives|publisher=Inner Traditions / Bear & Co|year=2010|isbn=978-1-59477-305-1|page=253|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RZV5f4EnTf8C&pg=PA253}}</ref> The seeds are so small that they are tedious to gather, but they can be ground into a flour substitute or extender.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Vizgirdas, Ray S. |author2=Rey-Vizgirdas, Edna |title=Wild Plants Of The Sierra Nevada|publisher=University of Nevada Press|year=2005|isbn=978-0-87417-535-6|pages=148–149|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4fYHi-Eyyt4C&pg=PA148}}</ref>

Plantain contains [[phytochemical]]s including [[allantoin]], [[aucubin]], [[ursolic acid]], [[flavonoids]], and [[asperuloside]].<ref name="drugs">{{Cite web|url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/plantain.html|title=Plantago|publisher=Drugs.com|date=2020-09-23|access-date=2020-04-18}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Duke, James A.|chapter=Plantago major|title=Handbook of Phytochemical Constituents of GRAS Herbs and Other Economic Plants|publisher=CRC Press|year=2001|isbn=978-0-8493-3865-6|page=471|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R5AhRgbW8UIC&pg=PA471}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Centre for Mediterranean Cooperation|title=A Guide to Medicinal Plants in North Africa|year=2005|publisher=International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN)|isbn=978-2-8317-0893-5|pages=190|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CBbU4Q0WYXEC&pg=PA190}}</ref> Plantain extract has been studied for its potential health effects.<ref name="Samuelsen-2000-p1" /> Plantain leaves were used commonly in [[traditional medicine|folk medicine]] for skin [[poultice]]s on wounds, sores, or insect stings.<ref name="Duke-2001-p151">{{cite book|author=Duke, James|title=Handbook of Edible Weeds|publisher=CRC Press|year=2001|isbn=978-0-8493-2946-3|page=151|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rVrteo-8cI0C&pg=PA151}}</ref><ref name="Green">{{cite book|author=Green, James|title=The Herbal Medicine Maker's Handbook: A Home Manual|publisher=Chelsea Green Publishing|year=2000|isbn=978-0-89594-990-5|pages=314–315|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5nxKJ7SocEUC&pg=PT314}}</ref> The root was used for fever and respiratory infections.<ref name="drugs" /><ref>{{cite book|last1=Foster|first1=Steven|last2=Hobbs|first2=Christopher|title=A Field Guide to Western Medicinal Plants and Herbs|publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt|year=2002|isbn=978-0-395-83806-8|page=224|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tg_bPUzhJ9oC&pg=PT247}}</ref>

100 g of fresh leaves provides 18.4 kcal from 2.29 g protein, 2.03 g net carbohydrates and 0.18 g fat. They are high in fibre with 3.88 g fibre per 100 g.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Guil-Guerrero |first=José Luis |date=August 2010 |title=Nutritional composition of Plantago species (P-major L., P-lanceolata, L., and P-media L.) |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261618820_Nutritional_composition_of_Plantago_species_P-major_L_P-lanceolata_L_and_P-media_L |journal=Ecology of Food and Nutrition |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=481-495}}</ref>
